content_definitions.template: This Food Safety Management System applies to {business_name} at {site_name}. The site operates as {business_type_with_article}. It explains the food safety controls, responsibilities, monitoring and corrective actions used for the chilling, temperature-control, cooking and reheating activities that apply to the business. It must be followed by all staff whose work can affect food safety.

{business_name} is committed to producing, handling and serving food safely at {site_name}. The business will provide suitable procedures, equipment, training and supervision; ensure that required checks and records are completed; and act promptly when a food safety control is not met. Food will not be served when its safety cannot be established.

content_definitions.text: Food safety is a shared responsibility. Everyone working for the business must understand and carry out the responsibilities relevant to their role.

items: The FSMS Responsible Person must maintain this FSMS, provide suitable resources, ensure staff are trained and supervised, and review the system when operations or risks change.
The person in charge of each shift must ensure that required checks are completed, records are accurate, and problems are acted on or escalated.
Food handlers must follow the approved procedures, complete assigned checks, report problems immediately and protect food from contamination or unsafe temperatures.
No member of staff may serve or continue using food when its safety is uncertain. The matter must be referred to the person in charge.

rows: Maintain the FSMS, provide suitable resources, ensure staff are trained and supervised, and review the system when operations or risks change.

content_definitions.text: Relevant food safety controls are monitored through routine operational checks and records. Checks must be completed at the time they are carried out and must identify the result, the person responsible and the date or time where required. Supervisors must review records and follow up omissions or repeated failures.

When a required control is not met, staff must first protect customers by stopping the affected activity where necessary and isolating affected food. The problem, decision and action taken must be recorded and reported to the person in charge. Food must be discarded when it cannot be shown to be safe.

This FSMS must be reviewed when the business changes its menu, processes, equipment or premises; after a food safety incident or repeated control failure; when relevant requirements or guidance change; and at suitable intervals to confirm that the controls remain effective.

sections.title: Business Scope and Food Safety Overview

content_definitions.template: The business describes its food operation as follows: {business_description_sentence}

content_definitions.text: The food activities within the current scope of this Food Safety Management System are:

condition_statements.statement: Keeping food chilled in fridges or chilled display units.
Cooling cooked food for later use or storage.
Defrosting frozen food before use.
Freezing food on site or storing food in freezers.
Preparing or cooking food on site.
Reheating previously cooked food.
Keeping food hot before serving.
Preparing ready-to-eat food.
Handling raw meat or poultry.
Cooking rice.
Using eggs or preparing foods containing eggs.
Cooking dried pulses such as dried beans.
Cooking or handling fish.
Cooking or handling shellfish.
Cooking or handling bread, bakery products, chips, fries or similar potato products.
Using a sink to defrost food.
Receiving food that arrives frozen.
Storing food that must remain frozen.
Using a microwave to reheat food.
Displaying hot food for service.
Using a slicer for cooked meat or ready-to-eat food.
Displaying chilled food for customers or self-service.

content_definitions.text: Based on the food activities carried out by the business, the principal hazards addressed within this FSMS are:

hazard_definitions.statement: Harmful bacteria growing when chilled, cooling, reheated or hot-held food is not kept under suitable temperature control.
Harmful bacteria surviving where food is not cooked or reheated thoroughly.
Cross-contamination between raw food and cooked or ready-to-eat food through hands, surfaces, utensils or equipment.
Food becoming unsafe through unsuitable storage, poor date control, incorrect defrosting or loss of temperature control.
Food-specific hazards, including parasites in fish, natural toxins in dried pulses and safety risks associated with shellfish.
Increased acrylamide formation where bread, bakery or potato products are cooked too dark or at unsuitable temperatures.

content_definitions.template: Food safety risks are managed through documented procedures, monitoring and corrective action. Where operational controls have been approved for {business_name}, they are set out in the relevant sections of this document. Staff must follow the controls relevant to their work, complete the required checks and report or correct failures promptly.

{business_name} controls chilled and frozen food at {site_name} to prevent harmful bacteria from growing and to ensure that food remains safe. Suitable equipment, approved working procedures, temperature checks and corrective actions are used for the activities carried out at the site.

content_definitions.text: Chilled and frozen food must be kept under suitable temperature control throughout storage, preparation, display, cooling, defrosting and freezing. Staff must follow the approved controls relevant to their work, minimise the time food spends outside controlled storage and take immediate action when a required temperature or procedure is not met.

Chilled food can become unsafe when it is kept too warm because harmful bacteria may grow. Some foods require lower storage temperatures or shorter storage periods and must be handled in accordance with their specific requirements.

content_definitions.template: Chilled food at {site_name} will be stored, prepared and displayed under controlled conditions. Chilling equipment will be operated correctly, food will be used within its safe shelf life and any lower temperature specified by the manufacturer or an approved food-specific control will be followed.

content_definitions.text: Fridge and chilled-display temperatures must be checked at least once each day, beginning with the opening checks. The configured check method for each item of equipment must be used. Where a digital display or dial is relied on, it must be checked periodically against an independent thermometer or clean, disinfected probe.

When a fridge or chilled-display temperature exceeds its required limit, affected food must not be assumed to be safe. Staff must check the food where necessary, move it to working equipment where appropriate, follow the chilling corrective-action procedure and record the incident and action taken. Food must not be used when its safety cannot be established.
Harmful bacteria can grow when cooked food is left to cool slowly. Food that will not be served immediately must therefore be cooled as quickly as possible before chilled storage or freezing.

Cooked food intended for later use will be cooled promptly using an approved method and placed under chilled storage as soon as it has cooled sufficiently. Hot food will be properly chilled before it is frozen.

The temperature of newly cooked food must be checked with a clean probe and checked again at suitable intervals to confirm that it is cooling effectively. A clean, disinfected probe must be used for every check.

Food that is not cooling effectively must be divided, transferred or cooled using another approved method without delay. It must not be placed in storage while still cooling inadequately. Food must be discarded where the time or temperature history means its safety cannot be established.

Food that remains partly frozen may cook unevenly, leaving the centre insufficiently cooked. Food can also become unsafe where its surface becomes too warm during defrosting or where raw food contaminates other food, equipment or surfaces.

Food will be thoroughly defrosted before cooking unless the manufacturer's instructions require cooking from frozen or another approved safe method applies. Defrosting will be carried out using the approved methods applicable to the food and the site.

Food must be checked before cooking to confirm that it is fully defrosted. The check must be appropriate to the food, including checking for ice crystals, checking the centre where necessary and confirming that poultry joints are flexible.

Food that is still partly frozen must continue defrosting and must not be cooked unless cooking from frozen is permitted. Food contaminated during defrosting must be isolated and assessed. Food that cannot safely be refrozen must be used immediately where safe or discarded.
Food can become unsafe where it begins to defrost, is frozen too slowly or is stored in unsuitable conditions. Prompt freezing and suitable packaging also help protect food from contamination.
Food intended for frozen storage will be frozen promptly, packaged suitably and kept frozen until required. Hot food will be properly cooled before freezing.
Freezer temperatures must be checked using the configured method for each item of equipment. The check must confirm that the freezer is maintaining the required frozen-storage temperature.

Where a freezer is outside its required limit, affected food must be checked and moved to suitable working equipment where appropriate. Food that has begun to defrost must not automatically be refrozen. It must be used promptly where safe or discarded when its safety cannot be established.

content_definitions.template: The temperature of active chilling equipment at {site_name} must be checked using the method recorded for that equipment. Actual temperatures must be recorded rather than ticks or general statements. A clean, disinfected probe must be used whenever food or pack temperatures are checked.

content_definitions.text: Any reading above the applicable equipment limit must be treated as a non-compliant temperature and must trigger the corrective-action process. Staff must establish the actual condition of affected food rather than relying only on the equipment reading. For a fridge incident, fresh fish must be assessed against its applicable 5°C threshold and other chilled food against the 8°C threshold. One shared out-of-range duration applies to all affected food. Food must be discarded where it exceeded its applicable safe limit and it cannot be confirmed that this lasted for less than four hours. The incident, assessment, decision and action must be recorded.
Record the actual temperature shown or measured. Where a reading exceeds the required limit, follow the corrective-action procedure immediately and record the incident and action taken.

content_definitions.template: {business_name} controls cooking, reheating, hot holding and the handling of ready-to-eat food at {site_name} to ensure that food is safe to serve. Approved procedures, suitable equipment, appropriate checks and corrective actions are used for the activities carried out at the site.

content_definitions.text: Food must be cooked or reheated thoroughly using the approved method applicable to the product. Food must be protected from contamination before, during and after cooking. Hot food must remain under suitable temperature control until it is served, and ready-to-eat food must be handled safely because it may receive no further cooking before consumption.

Proper cooking kills harmful bacteria that may be present in food. Food that has not been cooked thoroughly may be unsafe. Cooking does not remove allergens, and cooked or ready-to-eat food can still become unsafe through contamination after cooking.

content_definitions.template: Food at {site_name} will be cooked thoroughly using suitable, properly preheated equipment. Manufacturer's instructions will be followed where applicable. Raw food will be kept separate from cooked and ready-to-eat food, and the approved checks appropriate to each dish will be completed before it is served.

content_definitions.text: A clean, disinfected temperature probe must be used to confirm that food has reached an approved safe time and temperature combination. The thickest part, centre or several locations must be checked where necessary to identify cold spots.

Food that has not passed its required cooking check must not be served. Cooking must continue where this can be done safely, after which the food must be checked again. Food must be discarded where thorough cooking or a safe temperature history cannot be established.

Some foods require additional controls because they may contain specific bacteria, spores, natural toxins, parasites or other hazards. Certain potato, bread and bakery products also require controlled preparation and cooking to reduce acrylamide formation.

Food requiring additional care will be obtained, stored, prepared and cooked using the approved controls applicable to that food. Staff must follow any product-specific supplier or manufacturer instructions and complete the relevant visual, temperature, storage and traceability checks.

Staff must check the characteristics relevant to the food, including cooking temperature, appearance, texture, shell condition, product labelling, storage conditions and cooking colour. Acrylamide-forming foods must be checked to confirm that they have not been overcooked or burnt.

Food that does not meet its applicable food-specific check must not be served. Unsafe or damaged shellfish, inadequately cooked food and products that cannot be shown to have been handled safely must be discarded. Over-baked, burnt or otherwise non-compliant acrylamide-forming products must not be accepted or served.
Harmful bacteria may grow after food has first been cooked. Reheating must therefore cook the food again thoroughly rather than merely warming it.

Food will be reheated thoroughly until it reaches an approved safe temperature in the centre. Suitable equipment will be used in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Food will be reheated only once and will be served immediately or transferred directly to hot holding.

A clean, disinfected probe must be used to check the centre of reheated food. Large dishes and microwaved food must be checked in more than one location where necessary to confirm that no cold spots remain.

Food that has not reached its required reheating temperature must not be served or placed in hot holding. Reheating may continue where this can be done safely, followed by another check. Food must be discarded where it has already been reheated once or its safety cannot be established.
Hot food can support the growth of harmful bacteria if it is allowed to fall below a safe holding temperature. Suitable equipment and regular checks are required to keep food safe until service.

Food intended for hot service will be cooked or reheated thoroughly before being placed into preheated hot-holding equipment. Hot-holding equipment will not be used to cook or reheat food. Hot food will normally be maintained at 63°C or above.

Hot-held food must be checked with a clean, disinfected probe to confirm that it remains at 63°C or above. Checks must be carried out at suitable intervals and when there is reason to suspect that the equipment or food temperature has changed.

Food below the required hot-holding temperature must not simply remain on display. The approved time-limited exception may be followed where it applies and the time can be established. Otherwise, the food must be reheated thoroughly, cooled safely or discarded according to its time and temperature history. Food that has exceeded the permitted display period must be discarded.

Ready-to-eat food may receive no further cooking before it is served. Contamination, poor temperature control or use beyond its safe shelf life can therefore make it unsafe without another cooking step to remove the hazard.

Ready-to-eat food will be protected from raw food, dirty equipment, unwashed produce, hands and other sources of contamination. It will be stored at the appropriate temperature, used within its shelf life and handled with clean, suitable equipment.

Staff must check separation arrangements, cleanliness, date labels, use-by dates, storage temperatures and the condition of equipment used for ready-to-eat food. Slicers and other complex equipment must be checked after cleaning to confirm that no food residue remains.

Ready-to-eat food that has been contaminated, stored beyond its safe date or exposed to an unsafe temperature must not be served. Affected food must be isolated and discarded where its safety cannot be established. Contaminated equipment or surfaces must be cleaned and disinfected before further use.

Cooking, reheating and hot-holding checks must demonstrate that the approved control has worked. The check must be appropriate to the food and may include a time-and-temperature check, examination of the centre or thickest part, testing several locations, confirmation of texture or colour, or verification of equipment performance.

content_definitions.heading: Check procedure
content_definitions.text: The probe must be clean and disinfected before use. The centre, thickest part or several representative locations must be checked as appropriate. The actual result must be recorded where the relevant procedure requires a record. Visual checks may support the approved method but must not replace a required temperature check.

Food that fails a cooking, reheating or hot-holding check must not be served. Staff must continue the process where this can be done safely, correct any equipment or method problem and repeat the check. The food must be discarded when the required control cannot be achieved or when its safety cannot be established. The failure, decision and action taken must be recorded where required.
